messages.content: What is the freezing point point of water at a pressure of 10 kPa?

function.name: thermodynamics_calculate_boiling_point

message.content:
At 10 kPa the freezing (melting) point of water is only slightly below 0 °C – roughly **–0.4 °C**.  

This comes from the fact that the solid‑to‑liquid transition involves a very small volume change (≈ 10⁻⁴ m³ mol⁻¹). Using the Clausius–Clapeyron relation for the melting curve,

\[
\frac{dT}{dP}\;=\;\frac{T\,\Delta V}{\Delta H_{\text{fus}}}
\]

with \(T \approx 273\) K, \(\Delta V \approx 1\times10^{-4}\) m³ mol⁻¹ and \(\Delta H_{\text{fus}}\approx 6.01\) kJ mol⁻¹, gives \(dT/dP \approx 4.5\times10^{-3}\) K kPa⁻¹.  
From 101.3 kPa (freezing point 0 °C) down to 10 kPa (difference ≈ 91 kPa) the temperature drops by about \(91\times4.5\times10^{-3}\approx0.41\) K, yielding a freezing point of ≈ –0.4 °C.

So, at 10 kPa, water freezes at about –0.4 °C.
